title: Walk out onto the sea ice from Iqaluit
description: Frobisher Bay freezes solid enough to drive on, and spring is when the light comes back and the town goes out onto it.

title: Watch narwhal at the floe edge
description: Where the fast ice meets open water, narwhal and bowhead gather. You camp on the ice with Inuit guides who read it for you.

title: Walk into Auyuittuq and Mount Thor
description: Mount Thor has the greatest vertical drop on earth at 1,250 metres, most of it overhanging. Registration with Parks Canada is compulsory.

title: See Kinngait printmaking where it began
description: The co-operative here has produced Inuit prints since 1959 and is the reason the art is known worldwide.

title: Fly into Virginia Falls on the Nahanni
description: Twice the height of Niagara, in a canyon system reachable only by float plane. The first natural site ever added to the world heritage list.

title: Look for whooping cranes in Wood Buffalo
description: The largest national park in Canada and the only nesting ground of the whooping crane, which was down to 21 birds in 1941.

title: Ice road across Great Slave Lake
description: Public roads ploughed onto metre-thick lake ice each winter, with a posted weight limit and a speed limit set to stop the ice waving.

title: Walk the red cliffs of PEI National Park
description: Iron in the sandstone turns the cliffs and the sand red, against water warmer than anywhere else north of the Carolinas.

title: Eat oysters and mussels where they are farmed
description: Malpeque oysters come from a bay twenty minutes away, and PEI grows about eighty per cent of North America's cultivated mussels.

title: See Green Gables and the surrounding shore
description: The farmhouse that gave Montgomery the setting, with the Haunted Wood and Lover's Lane walks she used by name.

title: Drive to North Cape and the reef
description: The longest natural rock reef in North America runs out from the tip, walkable at low tide, with a wind test site above it.

title: Kayak among the Hopewell stacks at high tide
description: Six hours after walking the sea floor you can paddle sixteen metres above the same ground. Nowhere else changes that much twice a day.

title: Walk the Fundy Footpath
description: Forty-one kilometres of coastal wilderness with river crossings timed to the tide, and a reputation as the hardest trail in the Maritimes.

title: Watch the Reversing Falls change direction
description: The tide is strong enough to push the Saint John River backwards through a gorge. Published times tell you when it turns.

title: Eat and dance at an Acadian kitchen party
description: The Acadians were deported in 1755 and came back. The Tintamarre each August is thousands of people making noise about it.

title: Stargaze at Cypress Hills dark sky preserve
description: Hills the ice sheets went round rather than over, so the ecology is unlike the prairie below, and the sky is protected.

title: Paddle to Grey Owl's cabin
description: Twenty kilometres of paddling and portage to the cabin where an Englishman who claimed to be Ojibwe wrote about conservation in the 1930s.

title: Walk the Meewasin Valley along the river
description: Sixty kilometres of free trail along the South Saskatchewan, with seven bridges and the Bessborough hotel on the bank.

title: See the Athabasca sand dunes
description: The most northerly major dune field in the world, a hundred kilometres of sand on a lake shore reachable only by float plane.

title: Walk the Forks and the human rights museum
description: Six thousand years of meeting at the junction of two rivers, with a museum built to argue rather than to reassure.

title: Watch bison at Riding Mountain
description: An escarpment island of forest above the farmland, with an enclosed plains bison herd and a lake town in the middle of the park.

title: Look for whales off Brier Island
description: Fundy tides push nutrients up where the bay meets the Gulf of Maine, and humpbacks and right whales feed on the result.

title: Soak at Takhini hot springs under the aurora
description: Forty-two degree water outdoors at minus thirty, with a hair-freezing contest each winter that people take seriously.
